summary:
Amur Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia, where the UK government's country policy and information note of June 2025 records that same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, and the Russian constitution offers no specific legal protections for LGBT+ people.

Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were prohibited outright in 2023, when the law signed by President Vladimir Putin banned gender reassignment surgery and the change of gender markers on official documents; trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned the same year. A trans visitor has no lawful route to have their documents recognised or amended in Russia, and must travel on documents as issued.

Public expression 'promoting' non-heterosexual relationships or gender transition is punishable under the 'gay propaganda' law by fines or detention of up to 15 days, with repeated offences risking criminal prosecution and up to four years' imprisonment. The expanded statute expressly reaches anything "justifying" gender transition, which places statements about transition and visible trans self-presentation within the scope of the offence.

The Supreme Court's 2023 designation of the "international LGBT movement" as an extremist organisation opened criminal prosecutions carrying up to 12 years in prison, building on the 2013 propaganda law. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for participation in that movement or for displaying its alleged symbols as of 30 June 2025, alongside 81 people convicted of administrative offences in 98 court cases since January 2024 for displaying those symbols, mostly on social media. Charges are brought under both the administrative and the criminal codes.

Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 people in Russia were affected by enforcement of anti-LGBT+ laws, including convictions, detentions and extremism prosecutions. Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers. It warns all travellers regardless of personal characteristic of wrongful detention and arbitrary law enforcement, and notes that foreigners found guilty under the propaganda law face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement is escalating in volume as well as severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding.

The speed of the post-designation crackdown was documented by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night. The Moscow Times reported on 23 June 2025 that arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, and quoted a queer woman in St Petersburg describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation.

Detention itself carries lethal risk. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims. This is the protection framework available to those who leave the country rather than those transiting through it.
localsOnly:
Residents face a permanent bar on legal gender recognition: the 2023 statute prohibits both gender reassignment surgery and any change of gender marker on official documents, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in the same year. There is no domestic administrative process by which a Russian resident can obtain correctly gendered documents.

Same-sex marriage is unavailable, and the constitution contains no specific protections for LGBT+ people, so discrimination has no constitutional remedy. The UK country policy note of June 2025 treats these as the settled national position.

Displaying alleged symbols of the designated "international LGBT movement" is itself an offence, administrative or criminal depending on the charge. Human Rights Watch recorded 81 people convicted of such administrative offences in 98 court cases since January 2024, most of them for material posted on social media, and 101 extremism-related convictions overall as of 30 June 2025.

Coercive practices against trans people are documented at the local level. BBC Russian reported on 27 July 2024 on "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in the summer of 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no sources specific to Amur Oblast. Enforcement patterns described here are federal and apply nationwide, but whether oblast-level police or courts in Amur Oblast have handled propaganda or extremism cases at a rate above or below the national average is not sourced and remains unresolved.

No source in the inventory addresses screening of transgender travellers at Amur Oblast's border crossing points or airports, including whether passport gender markers are inspected against presentation, so any such risk here is not sourced.

Whether gender-affirming care remains obtainable in Amur Oblast through informal or unregulated channels after the 2023 ban is not sourced and remains unresolved.
